sections.instructions: Part 1. Questions 1-10. Complete the booking form. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

transcript: NARRATOR: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a holiday cottage company to make a booking. First, look at questions 1 to 10.
AGENT: Good morning, Larchfield Holiday Cottages, Tom speaking. How can I help?
CALLER: Hi. I'd like to book one of your cottages for a week in the summer, if you still have anything free.
AGENT: Of course. Let me take a few details first. Can I have your name, please?
CALLER: It's Anna Delaney. That's D, E, L, A, N, E, Y.
AGENT: Thank you, Ms Delaney. And the best phone number to reach you on?
CALLER: My mobile is the easiest. It's 0 7 7 0 0, 9 0 0, 4 1 8.
AGENT: Lovely. And how many people will be staying?
CALLER: Well, originally it was going to be six of us, but my brother can't come now, so it'll be five. Two adults and three children.
AGENT: Five, then. And when were you hoping to arrive?
CALLER: We were thinking Saturday the seventh of June, but my husband's work has changed, so it'll have to be the following Saturday, the fourteenth.
AGENT: The fourteenth of June, for seven nights. Let me look. We have two cottages free that week: Kingfisher, which is right in the village, and Heron, which is about a mile outside, near the river.
CALLER: Which one is bigger?
AGENT: They both sleep six. Kingfisher is a bit more modern, but Heron is quieter.
CALLER: Quiet sounds good. We'll go for Heron.
AGENT: Is there anything the cottage must have?
CALLER: Yes. A dishwasher would be nice, but it isn't essential. What really matters is a garden. The children need somewhere to run around.
AGENT: Heron has a large one, fully fenced. Will you be bringing any pets?
CALLER: Just one. A small dog. He's very well behaved.
AGENT: That's fine. Pets are welcome in Heron, but there's an extra charge. It used to be ten pounds a night, but it's gone up this year to twelve pounds a night.
CALLER: Twelve. OK, that's fine. How do we get the keys? Is someone there to meet us?
AGENT: Our office closes at four on Saturdays, so most guests collect them from the post office in the village. It's open until six.
CALLER: The post office. Great. And how do I pay the deposit? Can I do it by card over the phone?
AGENT: I'm afraid our card machine is being replaced this month, so at the moment we're only taking bank transfer. I'll email you the details.
CALLER: No problem. Thanks very much for your help.
NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 1.

sections.instructions: Part 2. Questions 11-14: choose the correct answer. Questions 15-20: which activity is available at each location? Choose from the list.

transcript: NARRATOR: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking to new volunteers at a wetland nature reserve. First, look at questions 11 to 14.

GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook Wetland Reserve. I'm Ruth, and I coordinate our volunteer team. Before we walk around the site, I'd like to tell you a little about how the reserve came to exist and what you'll be doing here.

GUIDE: People often assume this was always a natural wetland, but in fact it was a gravel quarry until the late nineteen-eighties. When the quarry closed, the pits slowly filled with rainwater, and it was a group of local schoolteachers, not the council, who first campaigned to protect the area. The council only bought the land some years later.

GUIDE: Today we have around ninety volunteers. Some of you will help with the bird surveys, but most volunteers, about two thirds, actually spend their time on habitat work: cutting back willow and clearing ditches. It's hard work, but it's what keeps the wetland from turning into woodland.

GUIDE: You don't need any experience. We do ask everyone to attend a short safety briefing before their first session. It used to be a full day, but we've reduced it to two hours, and it's held every Monday morning.

GUIDE: The reserve is open every day except Christmas Day. Entry is free, although we do encourage visitors to make a donation. Parking is the only thing we charge for, and that money goes straight back into conservation.
NARRATOR: Now look at questions 15 to 20.

GUIDE: Now let me explain what visitors can do in different parts of the reserve, because they'll often ask you. Starting here at the Visitor Centre, this is where families come for pond-dipping. We have nets and trays, and children can look at the insects and tiny creatures that live in the water.

GUIDE: Just beyond the centre are the Reed Beds. There's a raised boardwalk all the way through, and it's completely flat, so this is our wheelchair-accessible path. It's also the best place to hear warblers in spring.

GUIDE: If you follow the boardwalk to the end you reach the North Hide. It's a wooden shelter with windows facing the main lake. We used to run photography workshops in there, but the space was too small, so those now take place at the Boathouse instead. The North Hide is where our guided bird walks finish, and people stay on to watch.
GUIDE: Sorry, I should say the guided bird walks start at the Visitor Centre but are really based at the North Hide; that's where the guide does most of the talking.
GUIDE: The Boathouse, as I said, hosts the photography workshops, and they're very popular, so visitors need to book.

GUIDE: Then there's Willow Walk, the long path around the eastern edge. It's a shared path, and that's where you can hire a bike from the small kiosk at the entrance. Bikes aren't allowed anywhere else on the reserve.
GUIDE: Finally, the Meadow, beside the car park. There are tables and benches there, so that's our picnic area. Visitors shouldn't eat in the hides because it attracts rats.
NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 2.

sections.instructions: Part 3. Questions 21-25: choose the correct answer. Questions 26-30: complete the sentences. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

transcript: NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two students, Priya and Daniel, discussing a presentation they are preparing on vertical farming. First, look at questions 21 to 25.
PRIYA: So, Daniel, we need to decide on the focus. I know you wanted to cover the whole history of indoor farming.
DANIEL: I did, but having read more, I think that's too broad for fifteen minutes. The tutor said she wants depth, not a list of facts.
PRIYA: Agreed. What about concentrating on whether vertical farms can actually compete with traditional farms on cost?
DANIEL: That's the most interesting question, I think. Everyone talks about the environmental benefits, but nobody explains the economics.
PRIYA: Right. So what did you find on costs?

DANIEL: The surprise for me was that it isn't the buildings that are most expensive. It's not the labour either, because most farms are heavily automated. It's electricity, for the lighting. That's by far the largest running cost.
PRIYA: That matches what I read about the farm in the Netherlands. They only became profitable when they switched to growing herbs instead of lettuce.
DANIEL: Why herbs?
PRIYA: Because herbs sell for a much higher price per kilo, so the energy cost matters less. It wasn't that they grew faster. Lettuce actually grows faster.
DANIEL: Interesting. For our sources, should we use the company websites?

PRIYA: I'd be careful. They obviously want to present the best picture. I'd rather rely on the government report and the two journal articles. We can mention the websites, but only as examples of how the industry markets itself.
DANIEL: Fair enough. And how should we split the presentation?
PRIYA: I'm happy to do the introduction and the case study, if you take the cost analysis. You're better with numbers than me.
DANIEL: OK, that works.
NARRATOR: Now look at questions 26 to 30.
PRIYA: Let's plan the visuals. I think a single chart comparing costs would be clearer than lots of tables.
DANIEL: Definitely. We should also show a photograph of the inside of a farm. People don't picture how tall the racks are.
PRIYA: Good. And for the conclusion, I'd like to suggest that the technology will probably succeed first in cities, where land is most expensive.
DANIEL: Yes, and maybe mention climates that are too cold for outdoor farming for much of the year.
PRIYA: Nice. What about a practice run? The tutor has offered feedback if we send a recording by Thursday.
DANIEL: Let's record it on Wednesday, then. And we need to keep it within fifteen minutes. Last time we lost marks for running over.
PRIYA: I'll bring a timer. And let's prepare a handout with our references, so we don't have to read them out.
NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 3.

transcript: NARRATOR: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about the acoustics of concert halls. First, look at questions 31 to 40.

LECTURER: Today I want to look at why some concert halls sound wonderful and others, frankly, do not. For most of history, hall design was a matter of trial and error. Architects copied halls that musicians liked, without really knowing why they worked.

LECTURER: That changed around nineteen hundred, when a physicist called Wallace Sabine was asked to fix a lecture theatre at Harvard where nobody could understand the speaker. Sabine realised that the key quantity was reverberation time: how long a sound takes to fade away after its source stops. He measured it, rather unusually, using cushions borrowed from a nearby theatre, adding them to the room one by one and timing how quickly an organ note died away.

LECTURER: From those experiments he produced a formula linking reverberation time to two things: the volume of the room and the amount of absorbing material in it. Larger rooms reverberate longer; more soft material, such as curtains, carpet or people, makes sound die away faster.

LECTURER: And people matter a great deal. An audience absorbs so much sound that a hall can sound completely different when it is empty. This is why modern halls use seats designed to absorb roughly the same amount of sound whether or not someone is sitting in them, so that rehearsals sound like concerts.

LECTURER: Now, what is the ideal reverberation time? It depends on the music. For speech, you want something short, under one second, or the words blur together. For orchestral music, listeners generally prefer around two seconds, which gives the sound a sense of warmth and fullness.

LECTURER: Reverberation is not the whole story, though. The shape of the hall matters too. Many of the most admired halls are long, narrow rectangles, sometimes called shoebox halls. Their side walls are close to the audience, so sound reflects back from the side quickly, and this gives listeners a feeling of being surrounded by the music. Researchers call this quality envelopment.

LECTURER: Fan-shaped halls, which became popular in the twentieth century because they fit more seats with a good view, often perform worse here, because the walls angle away and send reflections towards the back instead.

LECTURER: A final problem is the echo. If a strong reflection arrives more than about fifty milliseconds after the direct sound, the ear hears it as a separate event. Curved rear walls are a common cause, because they focus sound like a mirror. Designers break up such surfaces with irregular panels, which scatter the sound in many directions. This scattering is called diffusion.

LECTURER: Today, before a hall is built, acousticians test the design using computer models, and sometimes a physical model built at one tenth of the real size, filled with nitrogen to reduce the absorption of high frequencies. Even so, most designers will tell you that the final adjustments still happen once real musicians start to play.
NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 4.
